claim: Chromosomes in multicellular eukaryotes are organized into a series of topologically independent loops called TADs.
source: The chromosomes in multicellular eukaryotes are organized into a series of topologically independent loops called TADs.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about chromosome organization in multicellular eukaryotes, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: In flies, TADs are formed by physical interactions between neighboring boundaries.
source: In flies, TADs are formed by physical interactions between neighboring boundaries.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fly boundaries exhibit distinct partner preferences.
source: Fly boundaries exhibit distinct partner preferences, and pairing interactions between boundaries are typically orientation-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pairing interactions between fly boundaries are typically orientation-dependent.
source: Fly boundaries exhibit distinct partner preferences, and pairing interactions between boundaries are typically orientation-dependent.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Head-to-tail boundary pairing generates a stem-loop TAD.
source: Pairing can be head-to-tail or head-to-head. The former generates a stem-loop TAD, while the latter gives a circle-loop TAD.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the topology resulting from head-to-tail pairing, supported by the experimental data and figures in the manuscript.

claim: Head-to-head boundary pairing generates a circle-loop TAD.
source: Pairing can be head-to-tail or head-to-head. The former generates a stem-loop TAD, while the latter gives a circle-loop TAD.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the topology resulting from head-to-head pairing, supported by the experimental data and figures in the manuscript.

claim: The Drosophila eve TAD is formed by the head-to-tail pairing of the nhomie and homie boundaries.
source: The TAD that encompasses the Drosophila even skipped (eve) gene is formed by the head-to-tail pairing of the nhomie and homie boundaries.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript (Fujioka et al., 2016) and confirmed by the experimental data presented.

claim: The nhomie forward replacement restores the wild-type physical and regulatory landscape.
source: The nhomie forward replacement restores the WT physical and regulatory landscape: in MicroC experiments, the eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle topped by a plume, and the eve gene and its regulatory elements are sequestered from interactions with neighbors.
evidence: This is supported by MicroC experimental data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the nhomie forward replacement, the eve TAD appears as a 'volcano' triangle topped by a plume in MicroC experiments.
source: The nhomie forward replacement restores the WT physical and regulatory landscape: in MicroC experiments, the eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle topped by a plume, and the eve gene and its regulatory elements are sequestered from interactions with neighbors.
evidence: This is directly observed in MicroC data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the nhomie forward replacement, the eve gene and its regulatory elements are sequestered from interactions with neighbors.
source: The nhomie forward replacement restores the WT physical and regulatory landscape: in MicroC experiments, the eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle topped by a plume, and the eve gene and its regulatory elements are sequestered from interactions with neighbors.
evidence: This is supported by MicroC data in Figure 3A showing reduced contacts between eve and neighboring TADs.

claim: The λ DNA replacement lacks boundary function.
source: The λ DNA replacement lacks boundary function: the endpoint of the 'new' eve TAD on the nhomie side is ill-defined, and eve stripe enhancers activate a nearby gene, eIF3j.
evidence: This is supported by MicroC data in Figure 3D and gene expression data in Figure 4.

claim: In the λ DNA replacement, the endpoint of the eve TAD on the nhomie side is ill-defined.
source: The λ DNA replacement lacks boundary function: the endpoint of the 'new' eve TAD on the nhomie side is ill-defined, and eve stripe enhancers activate a nearby gene, eIF3j.
evidence: This is observed in MicroC data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: In the λ DNA replacement, eve stripe enhancers activate the nearby gene eIF3j.
source: The λ DNA replacement lacks boundary function: the endpoint of the 'new' eve TAD on the nhomie side is ill-defined, and eve stripe enhancers activate a nearby gene, eIF3j.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 4 and quantified in Figure 5A.

claim: The nhomie reverse and homie forward replacements restore the eve TAD with a circle-loop topology.
source: While nhomie reverse and homie forward restore the eve TAD, the topology is a circle-loop, and this changes the local physical and regulatory landscape.
evidence: This is supported by MicroC data in Figure 6 showing restored TAD structure with altered contact patterns.

claim: In the nhomie reverse and homie forward replacements, the eve TAD interacts with its neighbors in MicroC experiments.
source: In MicroC experiments, the eve TAD interacts with its neighbors, and the plume at the top of the eve triangle peak is converted to a pair of 'clouds' of contacts with the next-door TADs.
evidence: This is observed in MicroC data shown in Figure 6A and 6D.

claim: In the nhomie reverse and homie forward replacements, the plume at the top of the eve triangle peak is converted to a pair of 'clouds' of contacts with the next-door TADs.
source: In MicroC experiments, the eve TAD interacts with its neighbors, and the plume at the top of the eve triangle peak is converted to a pair of 'clouds' of contacts with the next-door TADs.
evidence: This is directly observed in MicroC contact maps in Figure 6A and 6D.

claim: In the circle-loop topology, eve enhancers weakly activate genes in the neighboring TADs.
source: Consistent with the loss of isolation afforded by the stem-loop topology, the eve enhancers weakly activate genes in the neighboring TADs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 7 showing weak activation of eIF3j and TER94.

claim: In the circle-loop topology, eve function is partially disrupted.
source: Conversely, eve function is partially disrupted.
evidence: This is supported by denticle band defect data in Figure 5B showing increased frequency of defects.

claim: Fly boundary elements have insulating activity that blocks regulatory interactions when placed between enhancers or silencers and their target promoters.
source: In addition to subdividing the chromosome into a series of loops, fly boundary elements have insulating activity. When placed between enhancers or silencers and their target promoters, boundaries block regulatory interactions (Bell et al., 2001; Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fly boundaries subdivide the chromosome into loops by physically pairing with each other.
source: Studies dating back to the 1990s have suggested that fly boundaries subdivide the chromosome into loops by physically pairing with each other (Chetverina et al., 2014; Chetverina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and experimental evidence from chromatin immunoprecipitation, chromosome conformation capture, MicroC, and direct imaging experiments.

claim: Self-pairing interactions of fly boundaries are head-to-head.
source: Self-pairing interactions are head-to-head. This seems to be a common feature of fly boundaries and has been observed for scs, scs', iA2, wari, Mcp, Fab-8, AB-I, homie, and nhomie (Fujioka et al., 2016; Kyrchanova et al., 2008a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The two boundaries bracketing the eve locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail.
source: The two boundaries bracketing the even-skipped (eve) locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail, while boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript (Fujioka et al., 2016).

claim: Boundaries in the Abdominal-B region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
source: The two boundaries bracketing the even-skipped (eve) locus, homie and nhomie, pair with each other head-to-tail, while boundaries in the Abdominal-B (Abd-B) region of the BX-C usually pair with their neighbors head-to-head.
evidence: This is supported by previous studies cited in the manuscript.

claim: The eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle with a plume in wild-type MicroC experiments.
source: As shown in Figure 2, the eve TAD and the four Abd-B TADs have distinctive MicroC contact patterns. The eve TAD is a 'volcano' triangle with a plume.
evidence: This is directly observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The endpoints of the eve volcano triangle are delimited by nhomie on the left and homie on the right.
source: The endpoints of the volcano triangle are delimited by nhomie on the left and homie on the right, and within the eve locus (the volcano), there are additional enhanced interactions.
evidence: This is observed in MicroC data in Figure 2A.

claim: Contacts between sequences in eve and the neighboring TAD on the left (TL) are much reduced.
source: While the volcano triangle is generated by contacts between sequences within the eve stem-loop, contacts between sequences in eve and in the neighboring TAD on the left, TL (which contains multiple sub-TADs and six genes: CG15863, CG1418, Pal1, CG12133, eIF3j, and CG12134), are much reduced (L-ev in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claim: Contacts between sequences in the eve TAD and sequences in the large neighboring TAD on the right (TM) are suppressed.
source: There is a similar suppression of contacts between sequences in the eve TAD and sequences in the large neighboring TAD on the right, TM (which contains TER94 and Pka-R2; ev-M in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claim: Physical contacts between sequences in TL and TM are enhanced compared to those between eve and TL or TM.
source: On the other hand, as expected from the regulatory interactions observed for stem-loops in boundary bypass experiments (Kyrchanova et al., 2008a), physical contacts between sequences in TL and TM are enhanced compared to those between eve and TL (L-ev) or TM (ev-M).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 2A and is consistent with previous boundary bypass experiments.

claim: The eve volcano triangle is topped by a plume generated by preferential interactions between TADs to either side of the eve stem-loop.
source: Because of the preferential interactions between TADs to either side of the eve stem-loop, the eve volcano triangle is topped by a plume (L-M in Figure 2A).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2A.

claim: The four Abd-B TADs (iab-5, iab-6, iab-7, and iab-8) have distinctive MicroC contact patterns that differ from the eve TAD.
source: Like the eve boundaries, the TADs in the Abd-B region of BX-C region are connected to their neighbors by the boundaries at their base. As predicted from genetic studies on BX-C boundaries, each TAD corresponds to one of the four parasegment-specific regulatory domains. While the MicroC contact maps for the four Abd-B TADs resemble the contact patterns in the eve TAD, these Abd-B TADs differ from eve in that there are no plumes above their triangle peaks (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The Abd-B TADs are overlaid by a series of rectangular interlocking low-density contact domains, or clouds.
source: Instead, the Abd-B TADs are overlaid by a series of rectangular interlocking low-density contact (LDC) domains, or clouds.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2B.

claim: The iab-6 regulatory domain is flanked by clouds generated by crosslinking with its next-door neighbors iab-5 and iab-7.
source: As illustrated in Figure 2B, the iab-6 regulatory domain is flanked by clouds generated by crosslinking with its next-door neighbors iab-5 (5–6) and iab-7 (6–7), followed by crosslinking with neighbors that are a TAD away from iab-6, iab-4 (4–6), and iab-8 (6–8).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC contact map in Figure 2B.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the left endpoint of the eve TAD is no longer well-defined.
source: While homie still defines the distal (relative to the centromere) end of the eve locus, the λ DNA replacement does not function as a TAD boundary, and the leftward endpoint of the eve TAD is no longer well-defined.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, one new endpoint for the eve locus maps to sequences between CG12134 and eIF3j.
source: One new 'endpoint' for the eve locus maps to sequences between CG12134 and eIF3j (green arrowhead), which in wild type corresponds to the left boundary of the TL sub-TAD TL4.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, another endpoint maps to sequences between eIF3j and CG12133.
source: The other endpoint maps to sequences between eIF3j and CG12133 (blue arrowhead), which in wild type define the left boundary of the TL sub-TAD TL3.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 3D.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the eve TAD appears to flip back and forth between alternative endpoints.
source: These interactions are not as stable as those between nhomie and homie as the density of interaction dots is lower. Furthermore, they appear to flip back and forth between alternative endpoints (as indicated by the green and blue double arrows in Figure 3F) based on the MicroC contact profile, which is consistent with a mixture of (at least) two conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the MicroC contact profile in Figure 3D showing lower density of interactions and multiple potential endpoints.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the homie boundary does not contact the λ DNA replacement.
source: As shown in the virtual 4C at homie viewpoint in Figure 3B and E, the homie boundary interacts with the nhomie forward replacement, but does not contact the λ DNA replacement.
evidence: This is shown in the virtual 4C data in Figure 3E.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, eve stripe enhancers activate eIF3j expression in syncytial blastoderm embryos.
source: As shown in the HCR-FISH experiment in Figure 4 and quantitated in Figure 5, we observed a series of eIF3j stripes over a dark background in pre-cellular blastoderm embryos.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 4 and quantified in Figure 5A.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the highest levels of eIF3j expression correspond to eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7.
source: While it is possible to detect all seven stripes in λ DNA blastoderm stage embryos, their levels of expression are not equal. The highest levels correspond to eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7, while eve stripes 4, 5, and 6 are expressed at much lower levels.
evidence: This is observed in the HCR-FISH data in Figure 4.

claim: The stripe enhancers for eve stripes 1, 2, 3, and 7 are located between the eve promoter and nhomie.
source: Since the stripe enhancers for 1, 2, 3, and 7 are located between the eve promoter and nhomie, they are closer to the eIF3j promoter than the enhancers for stripes 4, 5, and 6, which are located downstream of the eve transcription unit.
evidence: This is based on the known genomic organization of the eve locus.

claim: The nhomie deletion did not have any obvious impact on the level or pattern of eve expression in blastoderm stage embryos.
source: While the nhomie deletion did not have any obvious impact on the level or pattern of eve expression in blastoderm stage embryos (see Figure 4), it seemed possible that eve activity was not entirely normal.
evidence: This is observed in the HCR-FISH data in Figure 4.

claim: In the lambda DNA replacement, the frequency of larvae with two or more missing ventral denticle bands is increased nearly twofold compared to nhomie forward.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, the frequency of larvae with 'severe' defects (two or more missing ventral denticle bands) in nhomie forward is similar to that in a WT yw control. In contrast, in the λ DNA replacement, the frequency of larval cuticles with two or more missing denticle bands is increased nearly twofold.
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in the lambda DNA replacement is significant at the p<0.01 level.
source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.01 level (one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claim: Inverting the nhomie boundary converts the eve TAD from a stem-loop to a circle-loop.
source: Since nhomie and homie pair with each other head-to-tail, the endogenous eve TAD is a stem-loop. This orientation dependence means that one can convert the eve TAD from a stem-loop to a circle-loop by inverting the nhomie boundary.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MicroC data in Figure 6A showing the altered contact pattern after nhomie inversion.

claim: The eve TAD is reconstituted by nhomie reverse.
source: Figure 6A shows that the eve TAD is reconstituted by nhomie reverse (compare with Figure 3: see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, the plume topping the eve TAD is gone and is replaced by a much more sparsely populated LDC domain.
source: In addition, consistent with our expectation, the plume topping the eve TAD is gone and is replaced by a much more sparsely populated LDC domain (purple double-arrow and above).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, eve forms an LDC interaction domain with TM on the right.
source: On the right, eve forms an LDC interaction domain with TM (ev-M).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, eve interacts most strongly with sequences in TL4 on the left.
source: On the left, eve interacts most strongly with sequences in TL4, and progressively less strongly with sequences in the sub-TADs TL3, TL2, and then TL1 (L-ev).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claim: In the nhomie reverse replacement, the TL TAD is re-established.
source: In addition to restoring the eve TAD, the TL TAD is re-established, indicating that the nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6A.

claim: The nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
source: In addition to restoring the eve TAD, the TL TAD is re-established, indicating that the nhomie boundary is important in defining both endpoints of the TL TAD.
evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of the TL TAD in the nhomie reverse replacement.

claim: The eve stripe enhancers in nhomie reverse are able to weakly activate expression of eIF3j and TER94.
source: Figure 7 shows that the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 7.

claim: In nhomie reverse, eIF3j and TER94 stripe expression is detected in only about half of the blastoderm stage embryos.
source: In addition, eve-dependent eIF3j and TER94 stripes are detected in only about half of the blastoderm stage embryos (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5A.

claim: In nhomie reverse, the frequency of embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is nearly twice that of nhomie forward.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, the fraction of nhomie reverse embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is nearly twice that in either yw or the nhomie forward replacement.
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in nhomie reverse is significant at the p<0.05 level.
source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.05 level (one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claim: The homie boundary pairs with itself head-to-head.
source: To test this possibility, we took advantage of the fact that in addition to pairing with nhomie, the homie boundary pairs with itself (Fujioka et al., 2016). However, unlike nhomie:homie pairing, which is head-to-tail, homie:homie pairing is head-to-head.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fujioka et al., 2016.

claim: Inserting homie into the nhomie deletion in the forward orientation converts the eve TAD into a circle-loop.
source: This means that it is possible to convert the eve TAD into a circle-loop by inserting homie into the nhomie deletion in the forward orientation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MicroC data in Figure 6D showing the circle-loop topology.

claim: The MicroC contact profile of homie forward is similar to that observed for nhomie reverse.
source: As shown in Figure 6D (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), the MicroC contact profile of homie forward is similar to that observed for nhomie reverse.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the MicroC data in Figure 6D and Figure 6A.

claim: In homie forward, the plume topping the eve TAD is absent.
source: The plume topping the eve TAD in wild type (Figure 2A) or in nhomie forward (Figure 3A) is absent.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6D.

claim: In homie forward, the eve TAD contacts TL and TM instead of being isolated from its neighbors.
source: Likewise, instead of being isolated from its neighbors, the eve TAD contacts TL and TM.
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data in Figure 6D.

claim: In homie forward, the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
source: Figure 7 shows that the eve enhancers weakly activate both eIF3j and TER94.
evidence: This is demonstrated by HCR-FISH data in Figure 7.

claim: In homie forward, expression levels of eIF3j and TER94 at the blastoderm stage are low and are observed in only about half of the embryos.
source: As was the case for nhomie reverse, expression levels at the blastoderm stage are low and are observed in only about half of the embryos (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is quantified in Figure 5A.

claim: In homie forward, the frequency of embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is twice that of nhomie forward.
source: In addition, the functioning of the eve gene when it is in the circle-loop configuration is not as efficient, and the frequency of homie forward embryos with two or more missing denticle bands is twice that of nhomie forward (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantitative data in Figure 5B.

claim: The increase in severity of cuticle defects in homie forward is significant at the p<0.05 level.
source: Taken together, the increase in severity of the cuticle defects is significant at the p<0.05 level (one-tailed t-test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the denticle band defect data.

claim: PREs were first discovered because they induce pairing-sensitive silencing of reporter genes.
source: PREs were first discovered because they induce pairing-sensitive silencing of reporter genes (Americo et al., 2002; Kassis et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of PREs to physically pair with each other may be their most important function.
source: More recent studies have shown that the ability of these elements to physically pair with each other may be their most important function (Batut et al., 2022; Levo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Boundary elements are responsible for defining the endpoints of TADs.
source: In contrast, boundary elements are responsible for defining the endpoints of these looped domains (Arzate-Mejía et al., 2020; Batut et al., 2022; Bing et al., 2024; Chetverina et al., 2017; Ibragimov et al., 2023; Stadler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Fab-7 is unusual in that it appears to be able to pair in both orientations.
source: Of the endogenous (non-gypsy) boundaries whose functional properties have been studied in detail, only one, Fab-7, appears to be able to pair in both orientations.
evidence: This is based on previous studies of Fab-7 boundary properties.

claim: Fab-7 boundary activity depends upon factors that have been implicated in the functioning of PREs.
source: However, Fab-7 may be unusual in that its boundary activity depends upon factors that have been implicated in the functioning of PREs (Kyrchanova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kyrchanova et al., 2018.

claim: Self-pairing interactions in trans may be largely responsible for the pairing of homologous chromosomes in precise register.
source: This make sense, as the available evidence suggests that self-pairing interactions in trans may be largely responsible for the pairing of homologous chromosomes in precise register (Erokhin et al., 2021; Fujioka et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Head-to-tail self-pairing would uncouple the loops on the two homologs and sister chromatids.
source: In this case, head-to-tail self-pairing would uncouple the loops on the two homologs (and sister chromatids).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the topology of head-to-tail pairing.

claim: Volcano triangles with plumes are rare in the non-repetitive regions of the fly genome (~30).
source: A survey of the MicroC contact patterns elsewhere in the non-repetitive regions of the fly genome indicates that volcanoes with plumes are rare (~30).
evidence: This is based on analysis of MicroC data across the fly genome.

claim: There are two volcano triangles with plumes in the Antennapedia complex that encompass the deformed and fushi-tarazu genes.
source: For example, there are two volcano triangles with plumes in the Antennapedia complex, and they encompass the deformed and fushi-tarazu genes (Levo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Levo et al., 2022.

claim: Most of the euchromatic regions of the fly genome are assembled into TADs whose MicroC profiles resemble that observed for eve circle-loops and the Abd-B region of BX-C.
source: However, since most of the 'euchromatic' regions of the fly genome are assembled into TADs whose MicroC profiles resemble that observed for eve circle-loops and the Abd-B region of BX-C, it is possible that much of the fly genome is assembled into circle-loops, not stem-loops.
evidence: This is based on analysis of MicroC data across the fly genome.

claim: If a significant fraction of TADs genome-wide are circle-loops, this would effectively exclude cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general mechanism for TAD formation in flies.
source: If, as seems likely, a significant fraction of the TADs genome-wide are circle-loops, this would effectively exclude cohesin-based loop extrusion as a general mechanism for TAD formation in flies.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the incompatibility of circle-loops with the loop extrusion model.

claim: Stem-loops in flies are formed by orientation-dependent boundary:boundary pairing.
source: In addition, though stem-loops could be generated by a cohesin-dependent mechanism, it is unlikely that this mechanism is operational in flies, as we have shown here and in Bing et al., 2024 that stem-loops in flies are formed by orientation-dependent boundary:boundary pairing.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented in this manuscript and cited work.

claim: In the most common version of the loop extrusion model, the mammalian genome is assembled into an alternating pattern of stem-loops and unanchored loops.
source: In the most common version of the loop extrusion model, the mammalian genome is assembled into an alternating pattern of stem-loops and unanchored loops (Davidson and Peters, 2021; Higashi and Uhlmann, 2022; Perea-Resa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the loop extrusion model.

claim: The alternating pattern of high-density TAD triangles separated by regions of low-density contacts predicted by the loop extrusion model is not observed in published mammalian MicroC data sets.
source: However, this crosslinking pattern is not observed in published MicroC data sets (Hsieh et al., 2020; Krietenstein et al., 2020). Instead of an alternating pattern of high-density TAD triangles separated by regions of low-density contacts, the TAD triangles are generally linked to both neighbors, just as in flies.
evidence: This is based on analysis of published mammalian MicroC data.

claim: There are few stem-loop volcano TADs topped by plumes in mammalian genomes.
source: Moreover, also like in Drosophila, there are few stem-loop volcano TADs topped by plumes.
evidence: This is based on analysis of mammalian MicroC data.

claim: The crosslinking pattern between neighboring TADs in mammals appears similar to that observed for circle-loops in flies.
source: Instead, the crosslinking pattern between neighboring TADs appears similar to that observed for circle-loops in flies.
evidence: This is based on comparison of mammalian and fly MicroC data.

claim: There are no obvious volcanoes with plumes in the high-resolution RCMC studies of Goel et al., 2023.
source: However, there are no obvious volcanoes with plumes in the much higher resolution RCMC studies of Goel et al., 2023.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the RCMC data from Goel et al., 2023.

claim: The MicroC profiles in the RCMC studies most closely resemble those seen in the Abd-B region of BX-C.
source: Instead, the MicroC profiles most closely resemble those seen in the Abd-B region of BX-C (c.f. the Ppm1g locus in Figure 4 of Goel et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on comparison of RCMC data with fly MicroC data.

claim: Compromising cohesin activity has minimal impact on the TADs in the Ppm1g region of the mouse genome.
source: Moreover, compromising cohesin activity has minimal impact on the TADs in this region of the mouse genome, as evidenced from the MicroC pattern before and after knockdown.
evidence: This is based on analysis of cohesin knockdown experiments in Goel et al., 2023.

claim: In the A/B compartment model, the chromatin state of each DNA segment determines whether it will assemble into a discrete domain.
source: According to this newer version of the compartment model, the chromatin state of each DNA segment determines not only whether it will assemble into a discrete domain, but also how the resulting domain interacts with next-door neighbors, next-next-door neighbors, etc.
evidence: This is a description of the A/B compartment model.

claim: The sequences included in the eve TAD and its patterns of interaction with neighboring TADs are essentially the same in NC14 embryos as they are in 12–16 hr embryos.
source: To begin with, the sequences included in the eve TAD and its patterns of interaction with neighboring TADs are essentially the same in NC14 embryos as they are in 12–16 hr embryos.
evidence: This is based on comparison of MicroC data from different developmental stages.

claim: In NC14 embryos, eve is transcriptionally poised, probably in most or all nuclei.
source: In the former case, eve is transcriptionally poised (Chen et al., 2013), probably in most or all nuclei, while in the latter case, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei (Nègre et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: In 12–16 hr embryos, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei.
source: In the former case, eve is transcriptionally poised (Chen et al., 2013), probably in most or all nuclei, while in the latter case, the entire eve TAD is silenced by a PcG-dependent mechanism in all but a few nuclei (Nègre et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nègre et al., 2010.

claim: The transition from potentially active to silenced does not impact the eve TAD or how it interacts with neighboring TADs.
source: However, this transition from potentially active to silenced does not impact the eve TAD, nor does it alter how the eve TAD interacts with the neighboring TADs that are (mostly) transcriptionally active at both stages of development.
evidence: This is based on comparison of MicroC data from different developmental stages showing similar TAD structure and interactions.

claim: In the CG3294 meta-loop, a TAD boundary located at ~2.0 Mb on chromosome 2L pairs head-to-head with a TAD boundary located ~2.8 Mb away.
source: Shown in Figure 8A is a 2.8 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 2L generated by the pairing of two TAD boundaries, labeled blue and purple (block arrows).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The pairing of the blue and purple TAD boundaries in the CG3294 meta-loop brings sequences in the TADs flanking the two boundaries into contact.
source: The pairing of the blue and purple TAD boundaries brings sequences in the TADs flanking the two boundaries into contact, and this generates two rectangular boxes of interaction indicated by the arrows (see also blue double arrows in the diagram on the right).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The pattern of interaction in the CG3294 meta-loop (upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream) indicates that the blue and purple TAD boundaries pair with each other head-to-head.
source: As shown in the diagram, this pattern of interaction (upstream-to-upstream and downstream-to-downstream) indicates that the blue and purple TAD boundaries pair with each other head-to-head, and this orientation generates a large loop with a circle-loop topology.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8A.

claim: The 2.2 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 3L is generated by four TAD boundaries.
source: The 2.2 Mb meta-loop on chromosome 3L in Figure 8B is more complicated in that it is generated by four TAD boundaries (indicated by blue, brown, green, and purple arrows).
evidence: This is observed in the MicroC data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In the bin/Mp meta-loop, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail.
source: As indicated in the accompanying diagram, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail as do the blue and purple boundaries.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claim: In the bin/Mp meta-loop, the blue and purple boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail.
source: As indicated in the accompanying diagram, the brown and green boundaries pair with each other head-to-tail as do the blue and purple boundaries.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claim: Pairing of the brown and green boundaries generates a large ~2.2 Mb stem-loop.
source: Pairing of the brown and green boundaries generates a large ~2.2 Mb stem-loop that brings sequences in the TAD downstream of the brown boundary, which contains the Dhc64C and CG1808 genes, into contact with sequences in the TAD upstream of the green boundary, which contains the CG3238 and bin (binou) genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.

claim: Pairing of the blue and purple boundaries generates a small stem-loop bubble that links sequences in the CG7509 TAD to the TAD containing the Mp distal promoter.
source: Pairing of the blue and purple boundaries generates a small stem-loop bubble that links sequences in the CG7509 TAD to the TAD containing the Mp distal promoter (blue arrowhead).
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of interactions observed in the MicroC data in Figure 8B.
